lesson.title: Jerk: The Derivative of Acceleration
lesson.summary: Jerk is the rate at which acceleration changes, j(t) = a'(t) = s'''(t), and it's what you physically feel as a sudden lurch when acceleration itself shifts abruptly, like an elevator starting to move or a car's transmission shifting gears.
lesson.body:
Two rides can have the same top acceleration and still feel completely different: one smooth, one jarring. The difference is how abruptly the acceleration changes. Jerk quantifies exactly that, the derivative of acceleration, and it's a real design consideration: elevators, trains, and roller coasters are engineered to keep jerk within comfortable limits, since large, sudden changes in acceleration are what passengers actually feel as an uncomfortable jolt, separate from the acceleration itself.

Jerk is defined as j(t) = a'(t). Since a(t) = v'(t) and v(t) = s'(t), jerk is also v''(t), and, most directly, s'''(t): the third derivative of position with respect to time. This is exactly the third derivative concept from earlier in this unit, applied to motion.

Continuing the running example, s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t gave a(t) = 6t - 12. Differentiate once more: j(t) = a'(t) = 6, a constant. Because the position function is a cubic, its third derivative is always a plain constant, so this object experiences the exact same jerk, 6 m/s^3, at every instant of its motion.

A constant jerk of 6 m/s^3 means acceleration should increase by 6 m/s^2 every second, and the numbers from the previous chapter confirm this directly: a(0) = -12, a(1) = -6 (an increase of 6), a(2) = 0 (another increase of 6), a(3) = 6, a(4) = 12, each step up by exactly 6. That consistency is not a coincidence, it's what constant jerk means in practice: acceleration climbing at a steady, unchanging rate.
